False Prophets
FAWLS PROF-its
noun phrase
From Old English fals (incorrect, deceitful, counterfeit) + Latin propheta, Greek prophêtês (one who speaks forth, a proclaimer of divine will). Scripture anticipates and warns against false prophets from Deuteronomy through Revelation: those who claim to speak for God but whose words do not originate in His mouth.

Biblical Definition

A false prophet is a person who claims to deliver divine revelation—whether predictive prophecy, oracles of judgment, healing words, or divine direction—but whose message does not come from the LORD. Scripture is relentless in its exposure and condemnation of false prophecy. Moses set out the definitive tests: if a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the thing does not come to pass, or if he speaks in the name of other gods, he is a false prophet and shall die (Deut. 18:20–22). Jeremiah’s sustained polemic against the false prophets of Jerusalem names their characteristic marks: they prophesy out of their own hearts, speaking visions of their own imagination (Jer. 23:16); they speak peace where there is no peace (Jer. 6:14); they do not stand in the LORD’s council (Jer. 23:22). Christ Himself warns with particular urgency: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 7:15). The wolf in sheep’s clothing is the defining image: external conformity masking predatory intent. The apostolic test is doctrinal: any spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not from God (1 John 4:2–3); any angel or man who preaches another gospel is accursed (Gal. 1:8). Revelation warns of the false prophet as an end-time figure aligned with the beast (Rev. 19:20), confirming that the false prophet is not merely a historical curiosity but an abiding threat to the church in every age.

Webster 1828 Definition

False prophet: one who pretends to divine inspiration or commission; one who falsely claims to utter God’s word—denounced throughout Scripture as a deceiver whose works destroy the flock.

expand to see more

FALSE PROPH'ET. One who falsely pretends to divine inspiration or commission; one who predicts events falsely in the name of God—who speaks what God has not commanded.

2. In the New Testament, a class of teachers who come ‘in sheep's clothing’ (Matt. 7:15), outwardly Christian in profession but inwardly contrary to the truth of God.

3. Distinguished from mere doctrinal error by the claim to divine authority: a false prophet does not merely teach wrongly but claims God as the source of his wrong teaching.

FALSE, adjective. Not true; not conformable to fact or reality; erroneous; unfaithful to duty or promise; deceitful; counterfeit—as applied to prophets, one who speaks what God did not say.

PROPH'ET, noun. In Scripture, a person illuminated by the Spirit of God to declare future events or to reveal God's will—so a false prophet is one who claims this illumination without possessing it.

Key Scripture

Matthew 7:15 — "Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves."

Deuteronomy 18:20 — "But the prophet, which shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die."

1 John 4:1 — "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world."

Jeremiah 23:16 — "Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Modern continuationist Christianity has largely abandoned the biblical tests for prophecy, treating vague impressions and self-reported words from God as beyond challenge and creating a culture in which false prophets flourish without accountability.

expand to see more

In Word of Faith and charismatic ministry culture, the biblical tests for prophecy (Deut. 18:22; 1 Thess. 5:21) have been effectively nullified. Prophets who predict events that do not come to pass are rarely held accountable; their followers are taught that challenging a prophet is “touching God’s anointed.” The result is a subculture of unchecked prophetic claims where congregations are manipulated by manufactured authority, where false healings and false predictions cycle without consequences, and where the word “prophet” has been stripped of the biblical seriousness that once made false prophecy a capital offense. The New Apostolic Reformation in particular has elevated hundreds of self-styled prophets and apostles whose claims to divine authority are tested against no standard except popular approval.

The confessional Reformed and cessationist response is twofold. First, the canon is closed: the gift of foundational apostolic-prophetic revelation (Eph. 2:20) has ceased with the completion of Scripture, so no contemporary claim to new revelatory prophecy has any standing before the church. Second, where the term “prophecy” is applied to lesser gifts of insight or exhortation, 1 Thessalonians 5:21 commands: “Test all things; hold fast what is good.” Every claim to speak for God must be brought to the bar of Scripture, and what departs from Scripture is false—however sincerely delivered, however enthusiastically received.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The compound false prophet names the most dangerous of counterfeits: not open enemies but those who wear the garments of the genuine while carrying a different fire.

expand to see more

Greek pseudoprophetes — false prophet; Matt. 7:15's term for the wolf in sheep's clothing; the New Testament's standard word for counterfeit prophetic ministry

Hebrew nabi sheqer — prophet of falsehood; Jeremiah's designation for those who speak out of their own hearts (Jer. 14:14; 23:16)

Greek pseudos — lie, falsehood; the root marking false prophecy not as mistake but as fundamental departure from truth

Hebrew zadon — presumption, arrogance; Deut. 18:20's word for the prophet who “presumes” to speak in the LORD's name without commission

Greek diakrisis — discernment, distinguishing; 1 Cor. 12:10's term for the gift of distinguishing spirits—the God-given capacity to identify false prophets

Usage

"The fruit test (Matt. 7:16–20), the doctrinal test (1 John 4:2–3; Gal. 1:8–9), and the fulfillment test (Deut. 18:21–22) are Scripture's three complementary tools for identifying false prophets; each catches different kinds of counterfeits."

"False prophets are not always openly anti-Christian: Christ's ‘wolves in sheep's clothing’ carry the correct vocabulary and wear the expected garments—the subtlety is precisely what makes them dangerous to the undiscerning."

"The church's response to false prophets is not merely doctrinal correction but disciplinary exclusion: Paul names false teachers explicitly, warns congregations against them (2 Tim. 2:17–18; Titus 1:10–13), and instructs elders to guard the flock from their influence (Acts 20:29–30)."
